title: Agent Cody Banks 2: Destination London
full_review:
Frankie Muniz is back in action as Cody Banks, a junior James Bond out to save the world yet again in the middle-of-the-road comedy "Agent Cody Banks 2: Destination London" (MGM).

Muniz stars as the titular spy kid, a CIA-trained teenager with a license to kill though he's too young to have a license to drive. More comedy-conscious than the original "Agent Cody Banks" (2003), the sequel finds the half-pint hero in pursuit of his former instructor, Diaz (Keith Allen), a rogue CIA operative who has stolen top-secret, government mind-control technology with his sights set on global domination.

Plucked from the CIA training facility disguised as a summer camp, the agency's director (Keith David) sends Banks to a prestigious music boarding school in England -- which strikes an uncanny resemblance to Hogwarts Academy without the Quidditch arena. With world security hanging in the balance, Banks must infiltrate its criminal-minded headmaster's (James Faulkner) plot to help Diaz in his sinister scheme to turn heads of state into puppet potentates.

Saving the day is the easy part, but faking it on the clarinet in front of the classroom of international child prodigies -- now that'll really make you sweat. Not to mention trying to avoid being tongue-tied in front of Emily (Hannah Spearritt), the love-interest flutist who turns out to be working undercover for the British Secret Service.

As with the "Spy Kids" franchise, the film's core concept of a normal teen secretly being a super-cool operative with an arsenal of high-tech toys at his disposal will obviously appeal to the cloak-and-dagger fantasies of any young viewer who likes his or her milk shaken, not stirred. However, the adolescent awkwardness that fueled the original is somewhat muted in the new film. Yes, Banks is an international young man of mystery, but he is also a typical 15-year-old who would rather tangle with terrorists than talk to a pretty girl.

In the first film, set in a suburban high school, Banks used his stealth skills to humble class bullies and to get dates with Hilary Duff; saving the world was of secondary concern -- priorities most socially challenged high schoolers could identify with. It spoofed spy-genre conventions as a way of creating the ultimate geek's fantasy. "Destination London" embraces those conventions with less satisfying results.

Keeping their romance appropriately tame, Muniz and Spearritt harmonize their fresh-scrubbed mugging as well as their wind instruments, but the lame script dictates that their performance be played strictly in minor keys. The rest of the spy symphony is a cacophony of silly sight gags, cookie-cutter chases and cardboard cliche characters, including Anthony Anderson as Banks' bumbling CIA handler who poses as a chef at the conservatory. Cynthia Stevenson and Daniel Roebuck return for brief bookend appearances as Banks clueless parents.

One of the few genuinely funny moments involves perhaps the most musically talented dog since Rowlf tickled the ivories on "The Muppet Show."

Of course, what the film is really about -- and what director Kevin Allen takes full advantage of -- are the James Bond-style gadgets that come into play during Banks' espionage escapades. For his next mission, however, it might be helpful if young Cody Banks, along with his Dick Tracy-like video wrist monitor and exploding breath mints, was equipped with a less formulaic script.

As for this misadventure, its "destination" will quickly be the video store shelf.

Due to frequent action violence and some crude humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
